title: No Single Roman Method — Short A

segments.text: There was no single Roman method of crucifixion.
segments.tts_text: There was no single Roman method of crucifixion.

segments.text: Ancient writers describe different structures and postures, binding and nailing, flogging in some cases, crossbeams carried in some cases, and different lengths of exposure. Rare archaeological heel nails prove that nailing happened in particular executions. They do not establish one universal pose.

segments.text: Crucifixion killed, but it also degraded status, exposed the condemned, and turned punishment into a public warning. Cicero describes Gavius's cross at Messana with Italy visible across the strait. Josephus describes prisoners crucified before Jerusalem’s wall during a siege—an extreme wartime account, not a universal procedure.

segments.text: The method could vary. The display of Roman power remained.

segments.text: For Jesus, the historical anchor is Roman crucifixion under Pontius Pilate. The surviving evidence does not recover his exact posture, injury sequence, duration, or one certain medical cause of death.
